title: Decolonising ELT

pts: Decolonising ELT examines and challenges the field's historical roots in colonial power structures and their continuing influence on current practice.
This connects directly to Unit 59's linguistic-imperialism content, moving from critical awareness toward active, deliberate reform.
This is a genuinely active, developing movement within the field, not a single settled program with universal agreement.

v: Three short statements on cards; chart paper

items: Present three statements: one of critical awareness, one of decolonizing action and one of rejection (see model language).
Groups discuss how each differs and which reflects their current practice.
Groups draft a working definition of decolonizing ELT in one or two sentences.
Compare definitions and note points of agreement and disagreement.
In a DIET, trainees compare their definitions with a short extract from Kumaravadivelu (2016).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Awareness: ‘English teaching has colonial roots, and we should know this.’
Action: ‘We will choose materials, methods and scholarship that centre our learners’ lives and our region’s knowledge.’
Rejection: ‘English is a colonial language and should not be taught.’
Decolonizing ELT means teaching English well while questioning whose knowledge, norms and voices the course treats as normal, and changing that where it excludes our learners.

blocks.x: Decolonizing is not rejecting English; it is changing how English is taught and whose English it is.

body: Purpose: to distinguish critical awareness from decolonizing action. Content: two steps on a staircase: the first shows a teacher with a magnifying glass (‘awareness’), the second shows the same teacher rearranging a bookshelf (‘action’). Style: simple and hopeful. Board version: two steps with labels.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for comparing group definitions.

blocks.x: Definitions written on chart paper and displayed side by side.

pts: ELT methodology and theory have historically been developed predominantly by scholars based in a small number of Western, English-speaking countries.
This series itself draws heavily on this canon — worth naming explicitly, per Unit 59's critical-awareness principle, rather than presenting as neutral or complete.
Decolonising efforts actively work to include and centre scholarship and practice from the Global South and Outer/Expanding Circle contexts.

v: A reading list, syllabus or bibliography in use

items: Choose a reading list, for example from a D.El.Ed. or B.Ed. English methods course, or from this book.
For each author, note where they are based and where their research was carried out.
Tally the results by region and present them as a simple bar chart.
Discuss which regions and voices are missing.
Find two works by scholars from India or the Global South that could be added, and justify each.
Audit a school or college library shelf for English teaching books.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: UK: 9 · USA: 6 · Australia: 2 · India: 2 · Other: 1
Prabhu, N. S. 1987. Second Language Pedagogy: an early account of task-based teaching developed in Bangalore.
Mohanty, A. K. 2019. The Multilingual Reality: multilingual education from an Indian perspective.

blocks.x: The aim is not to remove good scholarship from anywhere but to widen whose knowledge counts (Kumaravadivelu 2016). A similar audit of this book’s own references would show a strong Western weighting, which Unit 100 acknowledges.

body: Purpose: to show the geographic concentration of ELT scholarship. Content: a world map with circles of different sizes over regions, large over Britain and North America, small over South Asia, Africa and Latin America; a hand adds a new circle over India. Style: clean data-map, no exact figures. Board version: a rough outline map with dots.

Google Scholar (free) to find work by scholars in specific regions.

pts: Whose images, names, and life experiences appear in teaching materials carries real representational weight, extending Unit 13's coursebook audit further.
Decolonising materials work actively seeks genuinely diverse representation, not just superficial diversity within a still Western-centric frame.
This connects directly to Unit 24's avoidance of the single-culture trap, applied with more explicit, deliberate intentionality.

v: One coursebook unit; an audit sheet

items: Revisit the coursebook audit from Unit 13.
Go deeper: for each text, ask whose perspective tells the story, whose life is ‘normal’, and who is the visitor or the exotic other.
Distinguish surface diversity (different names and faces) from deep diversity (different perspectives, knowledge and values).
Rewrite one text so that a local perspective is central, not decorative, without simply swapping one single culture for another (Unit 24).
Learners write a reading text about their own village, town or festival for younger classes.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An original text (written for this book):

lines: Priya visits London for the first time. She is amazed by the Underground and learns to queue politely.
A: Priya has an Indian name, but the text treats London as normal and her as the learner of manners.
B: Surface diversity. The frame hasn’t changed.
Priya shows her cousin Tom from Leeds around the Mysuru Dasara. She explains the procession and teaches him how to find his way through the crowds.

blocks.x: The second text centres local knowledge while still using English for intercultural exchange (Gray 2010).

body: Purpose: to contrast surface and deep diversity. Content: two picture frames; in the first, a new face is placed inside an unchanged London-street scene; in the second, the whole scene has changed to a Mysuru street during Dasara. Style: bright, respectful. Board version: two rectangles with small sketches.

items: StoryWeaver (free, Pratham Books) for openly licensed stories set in Indian contexts.

blocks.x: Learner-written local texts collected in a class anthology.

pts: Some widely-taught methodologies (communicative language teaching, task-based learning) carry implicit cultural assumptions about classroom interaction that don't transfer universally.
This connects directly to Unit 25's principled eclecticism and particularity principle — methodology should be genuinely contextually adapted, not universally imposed.
This doesn't mean rejecting these methodologies, but examining and adapting their underlying assumptions where they don't genuinely fit a given context.

v: A description of one communicative or task-based activity

items: Choose a common communicative activity, for example a pair ‘opinion exchange’ or a mingling task.
List the assumptions it makes about classrooms, learners and teachers (see model language).
Mark each assumption as true, partly true or not true for your class.
Adapt the activity so that its learning purpose survives where an assumption does not hold.
Compare how the same activity would work in a Kannada-medium government school and an urban private school.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Learners can move freely around the room.
Class size is under thirty.
Learners are comfortable disagreeing with each other in public, including across gender.
Teacher talk should be reduced to a minimum.

blocks.x: Adapted version for a class of fifty-five on fixed benches:

lines: Learners discuss in fours on their benches, turning to the row behind; one spokesperson from each bench reports. The teacher models an opinion exchange first.

blocks.x: Bax (2003) argued that communicative teaching often ignored context; Holliday (1994) proposed methodology appropriate to its social setting. Adapting is not rejecting CLT or TBLT, whose purposes remain sound.

body: Purpose: to show a method adapted to local conditions. Content: a plant labelled ‘task-based learning’ being moved from a small pot into a larger local field; its roots are being gently spread to fit the new soil. Style: gentle, organic. Board version: a plant and two containers.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared bank of adapted activities.

blocks.x: An adaptation log in the teaching journal.

pts: Major international exams' standard-variety assumptions (Unit 78) and cultural content raise genuine decolonising questions worth engaging directly.
Some assessment bodies are beginning to actively address this, though meaningful change remains gradual and contested.
This connects assessment theory directly to this poster's broader decolonising frame.

v: Public sample papers from one international exam

items: Choose a publicly available sample paper, for example from IELTS or a Cambridge English exam (Unit 92).
Note the topics, settings and names in reading and listening texts.
Note the accents in listening tests and the varieties accepted in writing and speaking.
Check what the exam board says publicly about accents, varieties and cultural content.
Discuss what learners need to know to succeed, and what the exam may miss about their English.
Compare an international exam with a board examination paper in English.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A group’s notes (written for this book):

lines: Reading: urban settings in Britain and Australia; one text about Kenyan farming.
Listening: British, Australian and North American accents; no South Asian accent.
Writing: descriptors refer to effective communication rather than to a named variety.
T: So what do we tell learners?
S1: Prepare for these accents and topics, because the exam is high-stakes.
S2: But also say that their Indian English is legitimate, and the exam is one measure, not the whole truth.

blocks.x: Some exam boards have broadened accent ranges and topic sources, but change is gradual and debated (see Unit 78 and Unit 92).

body: Purpose: to show the standard-variety assumptions in international exams. Content: a headphone icon with several sound waves labelled by region, some solid and some dotted to show inclusion or absence. Style: neutral. Board version: a list of accents with ticks and question marks.

items: Official sample papers on exam boards’ websites (free).

blocks.x: Printed sample papers annotated in two colours.

pts: Decolonising teacher training examines whose theoretical frameworks and whose 'expert' voices are centred in professional development, including in a series like this one.
This series has drawn substantially on the Western applied-linguistics canon — a limitation worth naming explicitly rather than presenting as complete.
Genuinely decolonised training actively seeks out and centres a wider range of scholarly and practitioner voices.

v: DIET faculty, teacher educators, resource persons

items: Choose one training module, for example a state in-service module on English teaching.
List the theorists and experts it cites, the case studies it uses and who delivers it.
Identify where local teachers’ knowledge appears, and where it could appear.
Plan one change: a case study from a local classroom, a session led by a practising teacher, or a reading by an Indian scholar.
Invite teachers to write short case studies of their own practice for use in future modules (Unit 91).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Before: three sessions on theory, all citing Western scholars; one demonstration by an external expert.
After: one theory session that includes Prabhu and Mohanty; one case study written by a teacher from a Chikkaballapura government school; one session led by that teacher.

blocks.x: This book has drawn heavily on the Western applied-linguistics canon; decolonized teacher education would also centre practitioner knowledge (Kumaravadivelu 2016).

body: Purpose: to show teacher education drawing on a wider range of voices. Content: a training room with a circle of chairs; speech bubbles come from a teacher educator, a practising teacher, a book by an Indian author and a book by a Western author. Style: warm, inclusive. Board version: a circle with four labelled dots.

items: DIKSHA (free, Government of India) for state teacher-education content and teacher-created resources.

blocks.x: Printed teacher case studies circulated at cluster meetings.

body: When inviting a practising teacher to lead a training session, give her time and support to prepare, and credit her work by name in the module. Practitioner knowledge is taken seriously when it is treated with the same care as published theory.

pts: Actively seek out and include scholarship, materials, and perspectives from beyond the traditional Western ELT canon.
Reflect critically on whose norms and whose 'standard' are implicitly being centred in your own specific teaching practice.
This connects directly to Unit 25's principled eclecticism — decolonising awareness becomes one more genuine input into deliberate, informed practice.

items: Choose three areas: reading, materials and classroom norms.
For each area, write one concrete action for the term.
Identify what would count as evidence that you did it.
Share with a colleague and review together at the end of term. As Unit 25 argued, this is one more input to principled choice.
A school English department makes a joint plan.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s plan (written for this book):

lines: Reading: read one book or article by an Indian ELT scholar this term.
Materials: replace two coursebook reading texts with local texts written by learners or teachers.
Norms: stop correcting Indian English features that do not impede communication, such as ‘prepone’, and discuss them as a variety.

blocks.x: Evidence: a reading note, two new texts in the class file, and a short journal entry on how learners responded.

body: Purpose: to show decolonizing practice as a set of small, concrete actions. Content: three footprints on a path, each labelled with one action: ‘read’, ‘rewrite’, ‘rethink norms’. Style: simple and encouraging. Board version: three footprints drawn with chalk.

items: Google Keep (free) for a term checklist.

blocks.x: A planning sheet stapled inside the teaching journal.

pts: Decolonising ELT remains an active, evolving, sometimes genuinely contested conversation within the field, not a finished, settled program.
This poster offers a starting orientation, not a complete or final treatment of a genuinely large, complex, ongoing discussion.
This connects to this entire tier's consistent stance: engaging honestly and critically with genuine complexity, rather than false, simplified certainty.

v: Four short statements representing different views

items: Read four statements that take different positions on decolonizing ELT (see model language).
Participants stand near the statement closest to their view.
Each group explains its position; others ask one clarifying question.
Participants may move if persuaded, and explain why.
Close with a written reflection on what remains unresolved.
Run it as an online discussion forum for teachers in different districts.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: ‘Decolonizing ELT is urgent and should change everything we teach.’
‘It is important but must be practical; teachers have exams and syllabuses.’
‘Parents want their children to succeed in English; decolonizing may distract from that.’
‘The term is too broad; I prefer to talk about fair and context-sensitive teaching.’
I moved from the third to the second. I still think exam success matters, but I see that using local texts does not stop that.

blocks.x: Decolonizing ELT is an active, evolving conversation, not a finished programme. This unit offers a starting orientation, and holding it with humility is part of the stance.

body: Purpose: to show decolonizing ELT as an ongoing discussion. Content: four people standing at four corners of a room, arrows showing some moving; the centre is labelled ‘unresolved questions’. Style: calm, balanced. Board version: a square with four labelled corners.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) for an anonymous opinion poll before and after.

blocks.x: Four statements pinned in four corners of the room.

body: Choose one text you teach this month and ask learners: ‘Whose life does this text treat as normal? Could the same English be taught with a story from our town?’ Invite one volunteer to write that story, and use it the following year.

dek: Unit 98 of 100: applying this tier's critical, rights-based frameworks directly to English teaching practice — examining whose knowledge, whose norms, and whose voices are centred.

aims.x: This unit moves from critique to reform. Earlier units examined linguistic imperialism (Unit 59), native-speakerism (Unit 96) and linguistic rights (Unit 97). Decolonizing English language teaching asks what follows for practice: whose knowledge we teach from, whose faces and names fill our materials, whose methods we treat as universal, and whose voices lead teacher education. The unit presents decolonizing work as an active, developing and sometimes contested conversation, and it applies the same questions to this book itself.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what decolonizing ELT means and how it differs from critical awareness alone;
trace some colonial roots of English education in India;
audit reading lists, syllabuses and materials for whose knowledge and experience they centre;
identify cultural assumptions built into widely taught methods and adapt them to context;
evaluate international examinations from a decolonizing perspective;
identify scholarship and practice from the Global South to include in your own development;
plan realistic decolonizing steps for your own classroom or training programme;
hold these questions with appropriate humility and openness to disagreement.

why: Why this matters. This is where the theoretical threads of critical language awareness, World Englishes, and linguistic rights converge into concrete implications for everyday practice.

background.x: English came to India as a language of trade and then of government. Thomas Babington Macaulay’s Minute on Indian Education (1835) argued for English-medium education to create ‘a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect’ [VERIFY wording against a standard edition]. Gauri Viswanathan (1989) showed how English literary study was used in colonial India as an instrument of cultural authority. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s Decolonising the Mind (1986), written from Kenyan experience, made the case that language education shapes how people see themselves and the world. These histories do not mean English is simply a colonial language today. Indians have made English their own in literature, law, science and daily life (see Unit 78). They do mean that some habits of the field have colonial roots worth examining.

Alastair Pennycook (1998) argued that many current discourses of ELT, about the superiority of English, the deficiency of learners’ cultures and the expertise of the West, were shaped in colonial contexts and still circulate. Suresh Canagarajah (1999), working in Sri Lanka, showed how teachers and learners resist and appropriate English on their own terms. Adrian Holliday (1994) argued for appropriate methodology, fitted to the social context of each classroom, and B. Kumaravadivelu (2016) called for a decolonial option in which teachers of the periphery stop waiting for methods from the centre and develop their own. They disagree on much, but share a critical interest in where the field’s knowledge comes from.

India has contributed more to ELT than is often recognized. N. S. Prabhu’s Communicational Teaching Project in Bangalore (Prabhu 1987) was an early source of task-based teaching. Scholars such as Rama Kant Agnihotri, A. L. Khanna and Ajit Mohanty have shaped thinking about multilingual education, and NCF 2023 builds on this tradition in treating multilingualism as a resource (NCERT 2023). Decolonizing ELT in India therefore includes recovering and building on Indian and wider South Asian scholarship, not only critiquing Western work.

This book must be honest about its own position. Most of the references in its hundred units come from scholars based in Britain, North America and Australia, because that is where much of the published literature has been produced and where much teacher education, in India too, has drawn its reading. The book has tried to ground every idea in Indian classrooms, but a decolonizing reading would still ask it to include more voices from India, Africa, Latin America and South-East Asia. This unit names that limitation openly.

items: Reading-list audit. A regional tally of one reading list, with two justified additions from Indian or Global South scholarship.
Materials rewrite. One coursebook text rewritten to centre a local perspective, with a note on surface and deep diversity.
Method adaptation. One communicative activity adapted for a large class, with assumptions identified and purposes preserved.
Personal plan. A term-long decolonizing plan with evidence of progress.
Which of your teaching habits might have colonial roots? Which do you want to keep, and why?
Whose names appear on the reading lists that shaped your own training?
When did a method fail in your class because of an assumption it made?
How do you balance exam preparation with valuing learners’ own English?
Which Indian or South Asian scholars would you recommend to a new teacher?
What part of this debate do you find most difficult or unconvincing?

terms.def: Holliday’s (1994) argument that teaching methods should be fitted to the social and cultural context of each classroom rather than imported unchanged from elsewhere.
The influence that colonial history continues to have on English education, for example in attitudes about the superiority of English or of Western teaching methods.
Kumaravadivelu’s (2016) call for teachers outside the traditional centres of ELT to stop waiting for methods from the West and develop their own.
Examining and challenging the colonial roots of English language teaching, such as assumptions about native-speaker authority and Western methods, and valuing local knowledge and practices.

A broad term for countries of Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Pacific, often formerly colonized. In ELT it draws attention to scholarship and practice from these regions, including India, that are under-represented.

The unequal relationship in which ELT theory, methods and materials flow mainly from Anglophone ‘centre’ countries to the ‘periphery’, whose own knowledge and practice are under-recognized (Phillipson 1992).

An approach to teaching based on the postmethod condition and the parameters of particularity, practicality and possibility, which positions teachers as theorizers of their own practice (Kumaravadivelu 2001).
The knowledge teachers build from their own classroom experience and reflection, about particular learners, contexts and what works; it complements, and can challenge, findings from formal research.

The way people, places, cultures and languages are portrayed, or left out, in teaching materials. Critical review asks whose lives and perspectives a coursebook presents as normal, and whether Indian learners can see their own worlds in it.

The difference between adding diverse faces or names to otherwise unchanged materials (surface diversity) and reshaping content, perspectives and settings to centre other lives (deep diversity), for example setting a text in Mysuru during Dasara.
